# Relationalized Finance (Bollier and Hulst, 2025)

*An essay by David Bollier and Natasha Hulst of the Schumacher Center for a New Economics, version 1.0, dated 8 December 2025 (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 1, 28). It runs to 28 pages in five sections. Read for this page: the whole essay. The essay is by outside authors, and this page is a summary in our own words, not a copy.*

## What it argues

The authors propose a noncapitalist finance for bioregions, which they call relationalized finance (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 1). They argue that green finance, ESG screens, carbon offsets and similar strategies have left the core logic of finance intact. Growth, returns and investor control remain in place (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 1-2). They cite a 2025 nature-finance report: over $7 trillion a year finances harm, while under $200 billion goes to protection or restoration (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 2).

Relationalized finance exists to deepen social, economic and political relationships in a particular bioregion. It does not seek private financial gain (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 3). The authors describe it as "nonextractive, peer governed, place-specific, humane" (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 3). They judge state reform of finance a nonstarter for now, with some openings at municipal level (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 3).

The central proposal is a regrantor fund, one possible form of bioregional finance facility. It sits as a buffer between funders and commons, so money arrives without transactional demands on the people who receive it (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 22-23). The authors name the move of money from capitalist circuits into commons-stewarded value transvestment (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 3, 26).

## Key points

- **The problem is ontological.** In the authors' view, price cannot express the value of living systems, because that value lives in their relationships (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 10-12). Making nature measurable so that markets can price it is, they argue, a category mistake (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 12).
- **Commons as the vehicle.** Commoning gives people a proven way to govern shared wealth, limit extraction and meet needs fairly (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 7-8). The authors admit that commons can suffer from hierarchy, cliques and poor coordination (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 9).
- **Six premises for a bioregional economy.** They include inalienable shared wealth, federated structures, peer governance before trade, and commons/public partnerships with the state (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 7).
- **Socio-ecological markets.** Section 4 lists eighteen strategies, from land trusts and bioregional currencies to rotating savings groups, public procurement and community wealth building (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 16-21). Examples include BerkShares, Agrarian Trust and Terre de Liens (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 17-18).
- **How the regrantor fund works.** Money would pool from commoners, allies, crowdfunding, supportive businesses, philanthropy and local government. Trustees from the commons and bioregional community would make the grants (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 23). The model is the foundations behind open source software such as Debian and Apache (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 23).
- **Money stays at arm's length.** The fund follows a commoning pattern: "keep commoning and commerce distinct" (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 23). A strong culture of commoning has to come first.
- **Peer judgement over single metrics.** The authors argue that a single bottom line is the wrong test for this kind of finance (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 27). They point to peer certification, such as Barcelona's Community Balance and the Participatory Guarantee Systems used by agroecological farmers (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 27).
- **Coexistence with mainstream finance.** The authors say relationalized finance will not displace capitalist finance, and expect the two to coexist. Their bet is that its logic spreads and gains influence over time (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 25). Amsterdam and a citizen fund in Kingston, New York, are early experiments (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 27-28).

## Where it sits in this wiki

- [[Bioregional Financing Facilities (book, 2024)]]: the essay credits the BFF idea to Power and Seefeld's book (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, pp. 3, 21). It offers the regrantor fund as one type of BFF (raw/Relationalized_Finance_essay_version_1.0_December_8_2025.pdf, p. 22).
- [[SI-SF: System Investing and System Finance (Codex 25)]]: a contrast. Codex 25 builds tools to price value and route it through contracts and securities. This essay warns that pricing living systems distorts them (synthesis).
- [[BFF Discovery Arc 1: Allocation Decision Governance]]: regrantor trustees, flow funding and peer certification each answer who decides allocation (synthesis).
- [[BFF Discovery Arc 4: Multi-Capital Returns]]: the essay doubts that living value should be measured as returns at all. That challenges multi-capital accounting (synthesis).

# RZ Studio (rz.capital)

*The single-page website of RZ Studio at rz.capital. This page describes the site as read on 24 September 2026 (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, header). Read for this page: the whole page text. Linked documents were not read.*

## What it argues

RZ Studio describes its purpose as "Building place-based capital allocation capacity" (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, top heading). Its starting point is degenerative volatility, an era in which shocks arrive faster than institutions can adapt (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Context). It believes that partners with years of civic legitimacy and closeness to real risk are the best place to allocate to resilience (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Why).

With those partners, it proposes, tests and replicates the legal, economic and governance structures for durable allocation into foundational systems (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, What). The site states the mission as "to radically re-code capital allocation" (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, mission). Eight short position statements set out how it thinks about returns, risk, power and security (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, RZ Positions). The site lists a team of four, including Leon Seefeld and Indy Johar of Dark Matter Labs (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, team).

## Key points

- **Five ways of working.** The studio offers co-creation, networks, inquiry capital, shared intelligence and allocation capital (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, studio offer). Allocation capital is a conditional anchor allocation into new capital architecture (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Allocation Capital).
- **Grafting.** Its hunch is to join capabilities for a time at critical points of development, then spread new capacities through a small cohort (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, How).
- **Returns.** RZ holds that "every allocation of value, financial or otherwise, realises a return" (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Returns+). It explicitly rejects the language of return-seeking capital and market-rate returns (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Returns+).
- **Degenerative volatility.** The site's test: "when the interval between shocks is shorter than the time required to recover, the system becomes structurally fatigued" (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Degenerative Volatility+).
- **Security as continuity.** In a systems view, security means continuity: keeping energy, food, water and connection flowing through shocks (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Security+).
- **Holding risk.** RZ seeks to hold risk alongside partners, by sharing exposure and staying engaged. It treats this as developmental capital that builds a system's capacity to absorb risk (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Holding Risk+).
- **Necessary and possible.** Near-term, concrete goals serve as entry points. The lasting product is the systemic capability built on the way (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, Holding Necessary & Possible+).
- **Open questions.** These include multi-capital accounting, many-to-many agreements, systemic portfolios across whole bioregions, legal innovation and blended capital stacks (raw/rz-capital-2026-09-24.md, mission).

## Where it sits in this wiki

- [[The bioregions platform: programmes and pages]] records the launch of RZ Studio at a BioFi Deep Dive in September 2026.
- [[The Dark Matter Labs bioregions platform]] names RZ Studio as the way Dark Matter Labs allocates capital to place-based partners.
- [[The Believed Law of Financial Returns (Seefeld, 2026)]] argues, like the Returns position, against financial return as the organising principle (synthesis).
- [[Bioregioning as Critical Infrastructure (Seefeld, 2026)]] shares the vocabulary of degenerative volatility, foundational economies and security (synthesis).

# SI-SF: System Investing and System Finance (Codex 25)

*Codex 25 is a 74-page report from Dm Capital Systems, published in 2025 (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 1). Its named authors are Indy Johar, Leon Seefeld, Irina V. Wang and Raj Kalia. The report says it will be published in partnership with the TWIST team (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 4). Read for this page: the whole document in passes, from the contents and preface to the appendix (pages 1 to 74). Page numbers below are PDF pages, which match the printed page numbers.*

## What it argues

The report defines system investing as a strategy for changing whole systems, whether social, economic, environmental or a mix (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 4). System finance is the set of instruments, capital structures and governance models that make that strategy work (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 4). It argues that value structuring is an often overlooked bottleneck. It defines this as "organising and accounting for the value generated through large-scale interventions and converting this value to price" (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 15).

From there it builds a shared vocabulary. It covers what makes a system, value returns, investment strategies, capital structures, core functions and barriers (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 7-68). A fictional city, Ederfield, runs through the report as a worked case. The authors state that Ederfield is invented and draws on cities they work with (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 5). They describe their own frameworks as "at best, partially tested hypotheses that continue to evolve" (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 2).

In this view capital becomes a servant of the system and an enabler of other forms of capital (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 52). Metrics turn into tools for learning, and contracts become flexible agreements built on reciprocity (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 53-54). The report also treats democracy, culture, nature, rivers and bioregions as layers of quasi-infrastructure worth investing in (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 60-62). It states that it is not investment advice (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 4).

## Key points

- **What makes a system.** The report names four conditions: distributed agency, awareness of interdependency, shared purpose, and shared infrastructure for coordination (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 8). It also lists look-alikes that fail, such as a portfolio built to avoid correlation, or a monoculture held stable by subsidy (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 9-10).
- **Five layers of value return.** Input returns, direct value, spillover to nearby places, systemic outcomes like public health, and entangled macro-level outcomes (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 16-18). Pricing and sharing value across these layers is how the report proposes to make system programmes investable (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 18).
- **The Boring Revolution.** Three shifts: unbundled property rights, dynamic value chains, and structured economic systems where many actors pool resources and risk (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 19-23). Digital registries, smart contracts and algorithmic pricing form the backbone (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 25-26).
- **Four investment strategies.** Capability building, single-point investments with many beneficiaries, multi-point investments in one asset, and M3 portfolios (multi-point, multi-asset, multi-beneficiary) (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 30-33). The High Line in New York and Hawaiʻi Investment Ready's Food Systems Accelerator serve as real examples (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 30, 33).
- **Virtuous and stabilising portfolios.** Virtuous portfolios reinforce each other's effects. Stabilising portfolios buffer shocks in fragile systems and buy time for later change (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 34-37). The report suggests a portfolio of portfolios that shifts with the state of the system (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 37).
- **A 4x3 capital matrix.** Four stages of deployment meet three mechanisms: funds, transition financing facilities and monetary mechanisms (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 39). The stages run from capability building and deal construction to project financing and securitisation (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 39-40). Monetary mechanisms include new development finance institutions such as bioregional development banks (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 40). Funds alone are not enough, the report argues, and system finance often needs synthetic instruments (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 41).
- **Five core functions.** The first two are an outcome-stewards alliance of beneficiaries and an investors alliance. The others are a system or outcome accelerator, a system trust acting as public interest agent, and an independent governance and learning framework (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 45-50).
- **Barriers.** The report lists high interest rates, unpriced polycrisis risk, assets with no asset codes and bilateral contracts. It adds gaps in the capital stack, weak legitimacy and missing mandates for systems such as bioregions (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, pp. 64-66). System entrepreneurship also lacks dedicated risk capital and its own working methods (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 67).

## Where it sits in this wiki

- [[Bioregional Financing Facilities (book, 2024)]]: in the Ederfield case, the city co-founds a Bioregional Finance Facility with its neighbours (raw/DmCs_SI-SF_2708.pdf, p. 62). Codex 25 places such facilities inside a wider system-finance toolkit (synthesis).
- [[Relationalized Finance (Bollier and Hulst, 2025)]]: a contrasting view. Codex 25 builds tools to price value and route it through contracts and securities. Bollier and Hulst warn that pricing living systems distorts them (synthesis).
- [[BFF Discovery Arc 1: Allocation Decision Governance]]: the system trust and the independent governance framework offer one model for who decides allocation (synthesis).
- [[BFF Discovery Arc 2: Blended Finance and Catalytic Capital]]: the capital matrix and investors alliance frame how capital blends across stages (synthesis).
- [[BFF Discovery Arc 4: Multi-Capital Returns]]: the five layers of value return and the poly-capital idea bear directly on multi-capital returns (synthesis).

# Tay Bioregion Stocktake and Gap Analysis (2025)

*A 35-page report by Bioregioning Tayside and Dark Matter Labs, covering September 2024 to January 2025. It draws on ten conversations between two directors of Bioregioning Tayside and a lead from Dark Matter Labs. The report has no separate method or recommendations chapter. Its method sits in the introduction, and its suggested next steps sit in margin comments beside each answer. Read for this page: the whole report in three passes, covering the contents, introduction, summary table, all 15 element sections with their margin comments, and the appendix.*

## What it argues

The report asks whether the Tay Bioregion has the foundations a Bioregional Financing Facility (BFF) needs (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 4). It tests 15 elements of bioregional organising, learning from what other bioregional teams do (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 4). Its premise is that a BFF relies on a strong organisational base. Without one, existing financial interests could capture or misuse it (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 4).

The finding is that Bioregioning Tayside has deep local trust and a live project base, with few formal structures yet. It has no theory of change, no bioregion-wide vision, no regeneration strategy document and no integrated health metrics (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, pp. 5-6). Funding is the tightest limit, and the work is fully grant funded (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 6). Even so, the report judges the Tayside team "miles ahead of many other teams" (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 6).

The report also offers itself as a tool for other teams to gauge their own maturity. It avoids a fixed method for ranking gaps, because each place needs its own judgement (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 4).

## Key points

- **Fifteen elements.** The appendix defines each of the 15 elements (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 35). They run from the organising team and its theory of change to governance, finance, communication and links to other bioregions (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 35).
- **A small team carrying a lot.** The core team is small, and the directors do much of the work unpaid (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 5). Key-person risk is named as the most significant internal risk (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 10).
- **Projects without a portfolio logic yet.** Four projects were live, including the River Ericht Catchment Restoration Initiative and Feeding Tayside Through the Climate Crisis (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 18). Links between projects had not been mapped "in a strategic and systematic way" (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 18).
- **Funding and finance.** "Funding is the most significant constraint for BT at the moment." (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 6). No dedicated financial instruments or institutions exist in the bioregion yet (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 30). Nature finance in Scotland faces headwinds on verification standards, public policy and landowners' appetite for risk (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 9).
- **Weak bioregional identity.** People feel kinship at the scale of their community or their nation. The report notes that "Tayside as a place is not too much of a thing for people" (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 15). It links low care for land partly to the concentration of land ownership in Scotland (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 15).
- **Measurement.** No bioregion-wide health measure exists, and current metrics stand alone (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, pp. 6, 24). The team prefers to bundle carbon, biodiversity and social benefits instead of trading them separately (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 24). It wants restoration income to reach local people as well as landowners (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 24).
- **A distributed hub.** The team doubts the value of a single physical hub, which is costly to run (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 23). It suggests smaller dispersed spaces and a learning curriculum run through existing partners might suit better (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 23).
- **Next steps in the margins.** One comment proposes a regeneration strategy document that would become "the investment thesis for any BFF to be developed" (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, p. 21). Others propose an integrated health framework for a BFF, and growing Bioregioning Tayside's re-granting role until a dedicated institution can take over (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, pp. 24, 30).

## Where it sits in this wiki

- [[Bioregioning Tayside: the BFF page and interviews]]: the public account of the same project, which presents this stocktake as stage 1.
- [[Bioregional Financing Facilities (book, 2024)]]: the stocktake's questions cite page numbers in a book on BFFs (raw/tayside-stocktake-gap-analysis-report-2025.pdf, pp. 13, 16). It appears to be this one (synthesis).
- [[The Bioregional Health Framework]]: element 10 found no integrated health measure, and this framework offers one shared starting point (synthesis).
- [[BFF Discovery Arc 1: Allocation Decision Governance]]: element 12 found thin participation in decisions, the ground any allocation governance would build on (synthesis).
